progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c09 (carboxyl group, "-oic acid" names, salts "-oate", the hydrogen carbonate fizz test, acid hydrogen bonding and boiling points); chem-m7-c05 (alcohol names, the O–H and hydrogen bonding, boiling points, solubility); chem-m7-c08a (oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid with acidified dichromate under reflux); chem-m7-c08b (dipole–dipole forces from a C=O); chem-m7-c06 (why reflux: the condenser returns vapours; ethene hydration to ethanol); chem-m7-c03 (dispersion forces, "like dissolves like"); chem-m7-c02 (isomers; functional group isomers named in c08b); chem-m5-c03 (Le Chatelier: adding a substance shifts the position to use up some of it, removing one shifts it to replace some of it; the shift only partly cancels the change); chem-m5-c04b (a catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally and does not change the equilibrium mixture); chem-m5-c05 (K; author note only). Not assumed: ester, ester group, esterification, condensation reaction, alkyl alkanoate naming, separating funnel, the carbonate wash.

teaching.task: Banana and pineapple flavourings often get their smell from esters, and each ester can be made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. How do the two halves join and how is the ester named, why does the reaction never quite finish, how do you push the yield up and get the ester out, and how could you make it from ethanol alone?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) fruit smells come from esters, which can be made from an acid and an alcohol; three questions (1); (2) the acid loses OH, the alcohol loses H, they form water, and the parts link through the alcohol's oxygen: the ester group; condensation (2); (3) names: alcohol part first ("-yl"), acid part second ("-oate"); formulas are written acid side first, names alcohol part first; order matters (3); (4) working backwards: cut at the single-bonded oxygen next to the C=O; the C=O side is the acid (4); (5) no O–H, so no hydrogen bonds between ester molecules: low boiling point, volatile; isomers of acids, told apart by the c09 test (5); (6) slow, so a catalyst and heat; reflux keeps volatile liquids in; hazards (6); (7) reversible: all four remain; about two thirds (7); (8) excess reactant (some of it used up) or removing water shifts it right; the catalyst doesn't change the yield (8); (9) get it out: water dissolves most of the ethanol and sulfuric acid, the ester forms a layer, carbonate turns leftover acid into a salt in the water layer, dry, distil; the boiling point is only a rough check (9); (10) a two-step flow chart from ethanol; the main road, for a primary alcohol (10); memory aid (11); two attempts and brief feedback (12 to 15); handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: banana and pineapple flavourings often get their smell from esters, each made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, so the video asks how the two halves join and are named, why the reaction never quite finishes, how to push the yield up and how to get the ester out. The acid loses the OH from its carboxyl group and the alcohol loses the H from its OH, together making water, and the two parts link through the alcohol's oxygen: a condensation reaction. Ester names put the alcohol part first, ending in yl, and the acid part second, ending in oate, and working backwards cuts at the single-bonded oxygen next to the C=O. An ester has no O-H, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other; it boils lower than an acid or alcohol of similar size and evaporates easily, which is why it smells. The reaction is slow, so concentrated sulfuric acid is added as a catalyst and the mixture is heated under reflux; it is reversible and reaches equilibrium, so an excess of one reactant or removing water pushes the yield up (Le Chatelier's principle), while the catalyst only brings equilibrium sooner. The ester is separated with water in a separating funnel, washed with sodium carbonate solution to remove leftover acid, dried and distilled near 77 degrees as a rough check, and a two-step flow chart makes ethyl ethanoate from ethanol alone. The memory aid is acid plus alcohol in equilibrium with ester plus water, alcohol part first. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Banana and pineapple flavourings often get their smell from esters. Pentyl ethanoate is usually described as smelling like banana, and ethyl butanoate like pineapple. Each one can be made from two smaller molecules: a carboxylic acid, like the ones in the last video, and an alcohol. So how do the two halves join? Why does the reaction never quite finish? And how do you get the ester out?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "An ester has the condensed structural formula CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. Give the IUPAC name of the ester, and name the carboxylic acid and the alcohol used to make it." A skeletal formula is shown beside it in plain ink (no colours, no cut line). New ester (scenes use ethyl ethanoate, methyl propanoate, ethyl butanoate and butyl ethanoate); tests the cut, the order of the name and naming both reactants (the 2021 Q26 marker-reported trap: working backward from an ester). Crossed mistake: "propyl butanoate" (the halves swapped; the bank's "students most often swap the two halves"). (A2) "A student heats 0.50 mol of propanoic acid with 0.50 mol of methanol and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid under reflux. At equilibrium, 0.32 mol of methyl propanoate has formed. (a) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. (b) Suggest one change to the reactants that would give more than 0.32 mol of ester, and explain your answer using Le Chatelier's principle." New ester and data (scenes use ethyl ethanoate); 0.32 mol of 0.50 is a 64% yield, inside the site's range. Crossed mistake (Revision 2, science S1): "Heat it for longer, so more ester forms." (at equilibrium, more time adds no ester; the pack's rate against yield trap). "Add more concentrated sulfuric acid" is no longer crossed, because many texts and markers credit it (the acid takes up some water).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the production, in a school laboratory, of simple esters" This video explains the reaction, its conditions and yield, and how the ester is separated and identified; chem-m7-p05 carries out the preparation with its risk table (`C7-IQ2-05`). "draft and construct flow charts to show reaction pathways for chemical synthesis, including those that involve more than one step" This video introduces the flow chart with one two-step pathway (ethanol to ethyl ethanoate); chem-m7-c13 and g03 build and practise multi-step pathways. this video starts by naming the acid and alcohol parts of an ester, and stops at explaining esterification, its equilibrium and how the product is identified. It teaches: a carboxylic acid and an alcohol react to form an ester and water (esterification); the acid loses the OH of its carboxyl group and the alcohol loses the H of its O–H, these form water, and the two parts link through the alcohol's oxygen; the ester group –COO– (C=O then O then carbon); a reaction in which two molecules join and release a small molecule such as water is a condensation reaction; naming: the alcohol part first as an alkyl group ("-yl"), the acid part second ending "-oate" (as in c09's salts), ethyl ethanoate; condensed formulas are usually written acid side first while the name puts the alcohol part first; order matters (ethyl butanoate and butyl ethanoate are different compounds with the same formula); working backwards from a condensed formula: find the C=O and cut at the single-bonded oxygen next to it; the side with the C=O came from the acid (methyl propanoate from propanoic acid and methanol); properties: no O–H, so no hydrogen bonding between ester molecules, only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces, so for similar molar mass an ester boils well below an alcohol and a carboxylic acid (ethyl ethanoate 77 °C, pentan-1-ol 138 °C, butanoic acid 164 °C, all about 88 g/mol); small esters are volatile, which is why they smell; esters are functional group isomers of carboxylic acids, and only the acid fizzes with sodium hydrogen carbonate (c09); conditions: a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst, heat under reflux (c06 recall: the condenser returns volatile ethanol and ester); hazards: concentrated sulfuric acid is corrosive, the organic liquids are flammable, so heat electrically or with a water bath, not a flame; equilibrium: the reaction is reversible (water can split the ester back), so all four substances remain; from equal amounts of ethanoic acid and ethanol about two thirds becomes ester; Le Chatelier (Module 5): an excess of one reactant shifts the position right, using up some of it (with three times as much ethanol about nine tenths of the acid becomes ester); removing water also shifts it right, and concentrated sulfuric acid takes up a little water; the catalyst speeds both directions and does not change the yield; reflux keeps material in the flask and does not change the yield; isolating and checking the product: separating funnel with water (most of the ethanol and sulfuric acid dissolve in the water; the ester forms its own layer), wash with sodium carbonate solution (leftover acid becomes a salt that dissolves in the water layer, and CO₂ forms, so vent the funnel), separate, dry, distil, collecting near the ester's boiling point, which is only a rough check because ethanol boils at 78 °C; no fizz with carbonate shows the acid has gone; a two-step flow chart: ethanol oxidised to ethanoic acid (acidified dichromate, reflux), then ethanoic acid with more ethanol (concentrated sulfuric acid, reflux) to ethyl ethanoate, each arrow carrying reagents and conditions; the "main road" alkene, primary alcohol, acid, ester (only a primary alcohol oxidises to an acid). Not here: the practical procedure in full, quantities, the risk table and waste disposal (chem-m7-p05, with `C7-IQ2-05`); saponification, fats, oils and triglycerides (chem-m7-c12 territory; author note g); amides (chem-m7-c11); polyesters (chem-m7-c15); equilibrium constant calculations (author note d keeps the arithmetic); the site's avocado fat hook (site correction 3); reaction mechanism beyond which atoms form the water (author note b).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c09: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; main chain pale blue; branches amber; oxygen brick red; the functional group ringed red (the carboxyl group on acids, the O–H on alcohols, the ester group –COO– on esters); hydrogen bonds dotted violet; dipole–dipole attractions dotted teal; dispersion forces dotted pale blue; the acid side soft amber and the alcohol side pale blue only while the cut line shows; released water in the Module 5 water colour; conditions on arrows in navy. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Join them", "Name it", "Forces", "Conditions", "Yield", "Get it out", "Flow chart"); centre the structure board or reaction strip, one reaction or one ester at a time; the boiling point strip at the right only in scene 5; the yield bar under the strip only in scenes 7 and 8; plates small or medium at the left or right only in scenes 1, 6, 9 and 16. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous case leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 27 Oct by contact sheet): `m7-ester-fruit-v1.png` (a banana, a pineapple and a pear, side by side; scene 1); `m7-reflux-apparatus-v1.png` (a round-bottom flask on an electric heating mantle with an upright water-cooled condenser in a clamp stand; scene 6; the flask's liquid is painted amber, so it is labelled with the mixture's name and the colour is not mentioned; c06 and c08a reuse it the same way); `m7-separating-funnel-cloudy-v1.png` and `m7-separating-funnel-clear-v1.png` (aligned pair, identical alpha bounds: a stoppered separating funnel in a clamp stand, first with a cloudy mixed liquid, then two clear layers, a pale yellow upper layer over a pale blue lower layer; scene 9; the upper layer is labelled "ester layer"); `m7-school-distillation-setup-v1.png` (scene 9, small, for "distil"). Not used: `m7-perfume-bottle-v1.png` (the fruit plate carries the hook better); `m7-margarine-tub-v1.png` and `m7-vegetable-oil-bottle-v1.png` (fats are not taught here). No new plates. All plates small or medium, scaled uniformly only, never stretched. No human figures.
